News.title: I climbed onto Chernobyl’s roof with nothing but a lead sheet to protect me… I lived but was shunned for my heroism
News.content:
IT was known as the Stairway To Hell – a suffocating chamber leading to the roof of Chernobyl’s reactor four, which had been decimated in a deadly explosion.

Nearly 700 brave men ­huddled on the steps, armed with pickaxes and shovels, awaiting their turn to remove chunks of asphalt contaminated in the 1986 blast.





They could spend no more than two minutes at a time in the danger zone, which was bathed in a radioactive glow, or they would die.

As the 40th anniversary of the Chernobyl disaster in Ukraine approaches on April 26, the true story of sacrifices made by the clean-up team, known as liquidators, is now being told.

In total, around 650,000 men volunteered to help contain the nuclear fallout.

Russian scientists estimate that up to 125,000 had died by 2005, although authorities deny a definite link between the fatality rate and radiation exposure.

One of the surviving liquidators is 70-year-old Sergei Belyakov.

He reveals the only protection he had against radioactive residue was a lead plate hung around his waist as he climbed a ladder and then raced across the roof to get to work.

Clean-up crews were forced to play Russian roulette with their safety because hotspots loaded with fatal radiation levels could not be seen with the naked eye.

Sergei, who at the time was a chemistry professor and military reservist, got within 30 yards of reactor four, which spewed out dangerous waste that was carried on the wind across Europe.



Rain dumped the radioactive material as far as 1,800 miles away in Wales, and there was a ban on selling lamb which had grazed the contaminated land as it was not safe for people to eat.

Recalling his part in the clean-up mission, Sergei — who appears in National Geographic’s new documentary series, Chernobyl: Inside The Meltdown — tells The Sun: “On the staircase it was hell, it was completely stuffy, there was no air movement at all.

“The worst part of that is the unknown, anticipating what would happen to you, standing there for hours.

“Sometimes, I counted there were probably closer to 600-700 people coming through over the shift of eight hours.



“And every one there for the first time goes berserk, because they only got instructions when they came to the real job.”

At the top of the stairs, each man was handed a respirator, gloves and a lead plate to be hung around their waist, then given instructions on what to do.

The aim was to clear radio- active asphalt from the roof close to reactor four before it was encased in concrete to prevent further contamination.

Sergei says: “You go from one ladder, then run, go to another ladder, run up, climb again, run to the second place, and that’s what your place is when you have to start shoveling.

“I was a military chemist. I knew how to protect people.



“There’s certain materials which would protect you better than even the concrete wall. I ­understood the risks, but I did not understand the scale.”

The horror had unfolded as staff at the Chernobyl plant carried out a test on how reactor four would operate in a blackout.

What they did not know was that the cooling system had a design fault which was due to be rectified.

In the test, some 203 of 211 control rods, which prevent an uncontrollable chain reaction, appear to have been removed.

But they were reinserted during the process and the bottoms were coated in graphite, a material which caused a surge in the already unstable reactor core.



There was a rumble and a crack like thunder in the control room as reactor four exploded, killing two engineers.

A number of team members that tried to cool the reactor in the immediate aftermath died within weeks.

But some firefighters, including those in helicopters, who tried to bring down the temperature with more water, appeared to survive.

At first, residents of nearby ­Pripyat were not alerted to the danger.

Eventually, though, the 50,000 citizens of this “atom city” had to flee their homes for ever.



There was a news blackout in the Soviet Union, which Ukraine was part of at the time.

It was when Sergei saw the Dnipro river’s levels drop that he realised it was due to the water being used to cool the nuclear power plant.



He signed on for the clean-up operation against his wife’s wishes — and nothing could have ­prepared the senior lieutenant in the USSR’s 25th Brigade of Chemical Defence for the scenes of devastation at Chernobyl.

The air there had a metallic taste and the teams became aware that some areas carried a higher risk.

Sergei compared the intensity of radiation at the stricken site to a leopard — describing it as “spotty”.

He went on: “One of the things many people don’t know about Chernobyl is the radiation is not a steady thing. There were spots where the radiation was out of this world, like in the roof.”

Sergei reached his maximum exposure after six trips to the roof area, but he went another 17 times to the clean-up zone.



Clumps of his hair later fell out and his white blood cell level was close to zero.

The Russian Academy of ­Sciences estimated that 15 per cent of the liquidators had died by 2005, but this is often disputed.

The last of Chernobyl’s reactors was decommissioned in 2000 and the Zone Of Alienation around the plant became a ­macabre tourist destination.

Intrepid visitors were fascinated by the abandoned city, frozen in time.

But what Sergei saw in the immediate aftermath of the blast reminded him of a sci-fi movie.



He vividly recalls: “Very small levels of radiation propagate every living organism to start sprouting.

“We saw so many mushrooms — they were squishing under your feet, everywhere.



“There were trucks coming to my city, Dnieper, bringing ­potatoes from the Chernobyl area that were the size of watermelons.

“At the market, if people saw a Chernobyl license plate, they wouldn’t buy them.”

Ukrainian Sergei and other liquidators also faced hostility. He was shunned for fear he was still contaminated.

And he claimed that some involved in the clean-up were also resented because they received perks in acknowledgement of their role.

“When we visited Kyiv, we had gas mask bags with us,” he explained. “They immediately ­recognised that we are from ‘The Zone.’ Once that happened, the reaction was completely weird.



“As soon as the taxi drivers saw our gas masks, they drove off without us.

“Initially, people were understanding of how we suffered, because many of the people who were working there extensively got very high doses of radiation.

“But eventually, that turned into us being despised. We had a lot of benefits — free rides on public transportation, for instance.

“And when the Soviet Union was on the brink of collapse, there was a really big shortage of food, so people were angry with us because we got it.”

Sergei, who had one daughter before going to the disaster zone, was advised not to have any more children because they might be harmed by his radiation ­exposure. Incredibly, he recovered from his time in “hell”.



In 1992, he moved to the United States and, for the past 17 years, has lived in Singapore, where he is a managing director of a ­laboratory.

Despite what he witnessed at Chernobyl, ­Sergei is not against nuclear power.

“A lot has been learned from what went wrong in 1986 and Western technology did not have the same design flaw as Soviet equipment.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Sergei concludes: “I want people to understand what good nuclear power can bring, and what bad it can bring.”

News.title: London cops raid 4,000 cannabis farms in five years with sites including schools, hospitals and former police station
News.content:
COPS have raided 4,000 cannabis farms in five years in London alone.

The growing sites were at locations including schools, hospitals and at least one former police station.





Figures obtained through Freedom of Information requests show the borough of Enfield had most, followed by Barnet and Croydon.

Posh Kensington and Chelsea had the fewest.

Almost two in three cannabis farms were hidden in homes.

But Metropolitan Police data pinpointed four in properties labelled as a school or nursery.



Two were in a hospital or hospice and one in a place of worship.

One was in an emergency services building, and another in a property labelled as public, government or military.

One was found in a stables or riding school, and one at an estate agents. Two were discovered in hair salons.

Experts warn the drug farms pose a major fire danger due to the reckless way criminals illegally bypass electric meters heat and light the premises.



In August, a blaze at a house used as a weed farm needed around 80 firefighters using 12 engines to tackle it.

A London Fire Brigade spokesman added: “Cannabis factories are often in top floors or lofts which means when a fire takes hold, it spreads to neighbouring buildings.”

Det Supt Sean Lyons, the Met’s strategic drugs lead, said: “Drugs fuel violence and rip families and communities apart — that’s why we’ll continue to do everything in our power to tackle this criminality.”

News.title: Has Trump crossed a line by joining long list of wackos who take the Lord’s name in vain? I’m sick of cosplay Christians
News.content:
IT was, if you’ll pardon the pun, an almighty gaffe.

But let’s not clutch our pearls too hard — the current US President comparing himself to Jesus Christ was also textbook Trump.





The world’s Narcissist-in-Chief has ­considered himself in the top tier of humans since his first goo-goo-gaga.

You can just imagine his joy when he clapped eyes on that AI-generated “painting” of him, caught in the act of saving yet another lost soul.

“THIS IS WHO I AM, THE SAVIOUR OF THE WORLD”, his energetic ego will have assured him as assorted flunkeys guffawed along like demented seals.

Until, that is, someone was brave enough to tell him that it was, er, ­actually quite offensive to Christians and maybe he should take it down.

Yet while he may have taken this ­messianic monstrosity off his Truth Social feed, I’ll wager a crisp ten-dollar bill that it will appear in a gaudy gold frame on a wall at Mar-a-Lago before the week is out. The entrance hall, probably. Just to remind guests who they’re visiting.

BOW DOWN, LOSERS!

Meanwhile, “Doctor” Donald presumably just hopes God will, you know, forgive him his trespasses and all that.

Maga types were always going to go all in on burnishing their Christian faith, as they know it’s exactly what vast swathes of Americans want to hear.





The so-called Bible Belt takes in ten mostly Republican Southern states, including Mississippi, where 77 per cent of adults are Christian.

I’ve no doubt many Republican politicians have a firmly held belief in God.

I also have no doubt that some, like Trump, are just cynically exploiting this loyal voter base, many of whom truly believe their pumped-up prez is carrying out God’s will.

Not least during his latest adventure in Iran, where the mad mullahs would ­probably still send good Christians like them to the lions (or at the very least jail, as 73 were last year according to a recent report by International Christian Concern).

Yet this Christian cosplaying is not limited to the US — many prominent Brits, usually of the more swivel-eyed faction on the Right, have also drunk the communion Kool-Aid.

Like convicted fraudster Tommy Robinson, who claims to have “found Jesus” last year (while in prison, naturally).

Last week he appeared on a right-wing podcast, in his trademark Stone Island jacket, to hyperventilate about something called the “British Christian revival”, whatever that is.

What the big man upstairs thinks of the former English Defence League thug — with a penchant for snorting cocaine and punching people — using his name to advance his toxic brand of “politics” remains unclear.

And then there is Russell Brand, the former comedian, who made Christianity his latest obsession in 2024 after being baptised in the River Thames by oddball adventurer Bear Grylls (yes, you read all that correctly).

Cynical conversion

This week Brand announced he has another “booky wook” coming out, some sort of biography-cum-evangelical manual called How To Become A Christian In Seven Days.



Described, in typically Brandiose fashion, as a “testimony and guide to a timeless, yet zeitgeist-capturing, grounded, yet psychedelic encounter with Christ”, it is being published by fellow weirdo, Tucker Carlson.

This hyperactive author is of course the same Russell Brand that is covered in Hindu tattoos and credits Hinduism for saving him from a life of sex and drug addiction (and the same Russell Brand now facing charges of rape and sexual assault, all of which he denies).

Alas, preaching about Hinduism is no longer quite as fashionable as claiming to be a born-again ­Christian — and more importantly for brand Brand, not nearly as lucrative.

Indeed, at £25 a pop, Brand’s new tome proves that a conversion to Christ is the grift that keeps on giving.

For now, maybe.

But how much longer will the faithful tolerate their religion being treated as an accessory for the vainglorious or used as a fig leaf for the morally dubious?

Because if there is a God, I imagine he is getting pretty fed up with all these wackos taking his name in vain.

Certainly, genuine Christians are already starting to tire of these people.

This week’s backlash against Trump — who also found the time to slag off the Pope just hours before posting his ­ludicrous AI image — could prove, for want of a better word, prophetic.

Many prominent conservative Christians in the States are now suggesting that even the man who breathes belligerence has “crossed a line”.



As Riley Gaines, an influential 25-year-old American conservative activist, put it: “God shall not be mocked.”

Preach.

SHAME ON MUM 'N' DAD THE parents of the poor little souls slaughtered in the Southport massacre will live the rest of their lives in a mental prison of unbearable anguish. Meanwhile, the parents of the piece of shit that killed those children are living a new secret life somewhere in Britain at the taxpayers’ expense. Well, given that this week’s report into that horrific day in July 2024 has revealed that THEY are largely responsible for allowing their son to become one of Britain’s cruelest serial killers, is it not time to end that arrangement? What perks do we owe Alphonse Rudakubana and Laetitia Muzayire, who apparently cared not one bit about the safety of the citizens of the country that offered them safety? Yes, yes, I know they would probably be attacked if their whereabouts became known. But there is a simple solution to that. Authorities must do their damndest to find some way to charge them with a criminal offence and throw them in the slammer. And if that is not possible, they should be put on a plane back to their Rwanda homeland. I’m sure any crowdfunder for those flights would take minutes to reach its target. I’ll happily throw in the first tenner.

The Zuckerbot

META nerd Mark Zuckerberg has created an AI version of himself so he doesn’t have to bother dealing with his staff.

This Zuckbot will give presentations and take Q&As from his footsoldiers so he can spend more time getting kids hooked on “thinfluencers” and pretending to beat people up in his MMA octagon.

Some are aghast at this impersonal development, suggesting it is a grave dereliction of duty for a boss who claims to be all about “social networks”.

Hmm, I’m not so sure.

Having listened to the dry-as-a-bone, croak-voiced Zuck giving many speeches over the years, I’d be amazed if anyone could spot the difference between a robot and the real McCoy.

WHORE BLIMEY I HAVE spent many nights in Airbnbs but seem to have missed out on the ones that come with their own personal hookers. As The Sun revealed this week, it’s claimed some of the online firm’s rentals are being used by the oldest profession, much to their owners’ annoyance. So how long before someone launches a dedicated spin-off to avoid aggro for unsuspecting landlords? Just click here and download the app for . . . Whorebnb.

TFI CAN BE KEIR GENIUS

NICE to see TFI Friday making a comeback – an appointment to view for all us youths in the Nineties.



I wonder if they’ll bring back that odd fella who used to attempt something fairly straightforward each week and then make a hash of it?

“I tried . . . but I failed!” That was his catchphrase.

Seems unlikely.

Chris Evans and Co would probably get cancelled by the #BeKind mob for putting someone clearly on the spectrum under the spotlight in the woke-infested world of 2026 TV.

But there is an alternative – another man who also keeps on trying things, only for them to spectacularly fail.

Just need to check whether Sir Keir Starmer is free every Friday night at 11pm.

FIFA ON A ROLL I WAS in Mexico City this week – sadly a few months too early to spend thousands on a seat for the World Cup. But I can report that while the city’s airport still resembles a construction site, they are 100 per cent prepared for a Gary Lineker-style brown shorts incident.

WHEN I bought my first ticket for the National Lottery on its launch in 1994, I immediately felt a sense of dread.

What if I won? Would I turn into a pompous loadsamoney snob like Charles Frere from Howard’s Way?

Well, it turned out it was not me that week and I remained a skint teenager.

Fast-forward three decades and I’m now champing at the bit to get my hands on a ticket for the new BILLION QUID prize.



Just think of what I could buy with all that cash – council tax, gas and electricity, road tax, a tank of petrol – and maybe, just maybe, have a few bob left over to buy a second-hand Nissan Micra.

News.title: Two arrested after synagogue targeted in attempted firebombing as cops label it antisemitic hate crime
News.content:
SHAMEFUL ACT Two arrested after synagogue targeted in attempted firebombing as cops label it antisemitic hate crime

POLICE have arrested two suspects in connection with an alleged attempted arson attack that targeted a synagogue on Tuesday.

Cops said the incident is being treated as an antisemitic hate crime.





Police arrested a 47-year-old woman at an address in Watford and a 46-year-old man in the same area.

They are both suspected of arson endangering life.

It comes after a suspected failed firebomb attack at Finchley Reform Synagogue, in London, just after midnight Tuesday night.

Police said CCTV showed two balaclava-clad people dressed in dark clothing entered the synagogue’s grounds in the early hours of Wednesday morning, at around nine minutes past midnight.

News.title: Protesters demand cops release description of suspects who ‘gang raped woman outside church’ after she left nightclub
News.content:
HUNDREDS of protesters have gathered in Epsom demanding the police release descriptions of men suspected of raping a woman outside a church.

Riot police have been sent to the protest which comes after the alleged rape in the early hours of Saturday.





The woman, in her 20s, was reportedly grabbed by four men after she left Labrynth Nightclub and carried to the Epsom Methodist Church on Ashley Road.

Four days after the alleged attack locals have taken to the streets and demanded the police provide answers.

Surrey Police urged people not to speculate about the descriptions of the suspects and said the force do not have enough information to release descriptions of the suspects.

Around 100 officers in helmets and shields have blocked the High Street.



Billy Cooper, 39, said he finds it “disgusting” that cops have still not arrested anybody.

He told The Sun: “It is madness. This is an area where this sort of thing doesn’t happen. A gang rape here is unheard of.”

A private carer called Emma said she moved to Epsom 20 years ago from London because she thought it would be safer to raise her children and said the incident has “terrified” residents.

She said: “Why haven’t they arrested anyone? It’s been five days. The community is terrified. I don’t think girls living here will be brave enough to go out this weekend.”



Surrey Police released an update following the demonstrators: “We are aware that there is continued concern amongst the local community following a report of a rape which we received in the early hours on Saturday (11 April).

“We would like to reassure you that we are working diligently to establish the sequence of events and to clarify the circumstances and the details of those involved in the incident which is reported to have taken place between 2am and 4am outside Epsom Methodist Church on Ashley Road.”

East Surrey Chief Superintendent Mark Chapman said: “I understand the distress and concern that this incident has caused, both for the victim herself and amongst our local communities, and I want you to reassure you that we are working hard to progress this investigation.

“While we have already carried out extensive enquiries, we do not have sufficient information at this time to update you with the descriptions of the suspects. I appreciate that this causes increased concern, and I can assure you that we will update you with these descriptions as soon as we are able to do so.

“In the meantime, I would urge people not to speculate about the descriptions of these suspects as this may lead to additional tensions within our local communities.



“I would also like to reassure you that we have stepped up patrols in the area, and this increased police presence will continue over the weekend.

“While we continue to progress our investigation, we would urge anyone with any information who has not already come forward to do so as a matter of urgency.”

If you were in the area around Ashley Road, Epsom Methodist Church, or Labyrinth nightclub between 2am and 4am on Saturday morning, if you saw or spoke to a woman in her 20s in distress in this area, or you have any CCTV, dashcam, or helmet cam footage of this area during this timeframe, please contact us quoting PR/45260041426 or using our online form.

News.title: Moment US sailors turn back tanker that tries to break Strait of Hormuz blockade as they warn ‘prepare to be boarded’
News.content:
THIS is the moment US warships turned back oil tankers attempting to break through a newly imposed blockade off Iran – warning vessels to change course or face interception.

The dramatic enforcement came within hours of the operation beginning, as a US destroyer intercepted two tankers leaving Iran and ordered them to turn around.





The ships had departed Chabahar port but were stopped by radio communication and forced to head back, a US official said.

An audio clip released by the US military shows sailors saying: “The US has announced a formal blockade of Iranian ports and coastal areas.

“This is illegal action. All vessels are advised to immediately return to port if leaving and discontinue transit to Iran, if that’s your next border call.

“Do not attempt to breach the blockade. Vessels will be boarded and interdiction seizure transiting to and from Iranian port.



“Turn around prepare to be boarded. We do not comply with this blockade but we will use force.

“The whole of the United States is ready for force compliance. Out.”

They are among at least six vessels already made to reverse course since the blockade came into force.

The operation – described by US commanders as “fully implemented” within 36 hours – is designed to choke off Iran’s economy, which relies heavily on oil exports by sea.



US Central Command said it had “completely halted economic trade going in and out of Iran by sea” within the first 36 hours.

Military chiefs say no ships made it past the blockade in its opening phase, with multiple vessels complying with orders to turn back as a fleet of around 15 warships and 10,000 personnel patrol the region.

The US blockade is being enforced beyond the Strait of Hormuz, with forces tracking ships leaving Iran and intercepting them in open waters.

It applies to vessels linked to Iranian ports, with limited exceptions, leaving crews unsure whether they will be allowed through or forced to turn back.

Early data shows ships already reversing course or going dark, as the blockade begins to hit Iran’s oil exports.



Several Iran-linked vessels have been spotted slipping through the strait in the early hours of the operation, with some tankers linked to China and sanctioned ships continuing to move despite the threat of interception.

Another tense radio exchange in the Strait of Hormuz this week exposed the escalating confrontation between US and Iranian forces.

The exchange was captured by a sailor in the region after weeks of mounting tension in and around the Strait of Hormuz.

It was broadcast over Marine VHF Channel 16 – the international emergency frequency monitored by all vessels – with crews in the area already familiar with repeated Iranian warnings since the start of the conflict.

“Engaged in transit passage in accordance with international law,” a US-linked voice said over emergency Channel 16.



An Iranian response followed: “You are heading to the Persian Gulf and it is against Iranian law, so I advise you to alter course, go back to the Indian Ocean immediately.

“Go back to the Indian Ocean immediately. If you don’t obey my orders, I will open fire immediately. Out.”

Iranian forces then issued a wider warning: “Attention all vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf. You must clear this area as soon as possible, because we are targeting a US Navy warship in the area.”

The US vessel did not alter course.

“I intend to transit through Omani territorial waters and defend my unit if interfered with,” the US officer replied.



“No challenge is intended to you and I intend to abide by the rules of our government ceasefire.”

Military officials say ships are being tracked as they leave Iranian waters and intercepted further out in the Gulf of Oman.

Shipping data suggests the impact has been immediate.

Traffic through the strait has dropped sharply from more than 130 vessels a day before the conflict to single digits.

Some ships have turned around after clearing the waterway, while others have halted or reduced movement.



Analysts say vessels linked to Iranian oil are increasingly attempting to evade detection by switching off tracking systems or broadcasting false positions.

Iran had already disrupted shipping through threats and attacks, effectively closing the strait and cutting off around 20 per cent of global oil supply.

Vessels have been targeted with drones and projectiles, killing 11 crew members.

Its military has threatened to expand the conflict if the blockade continues.

Experts say it is too early to judge the effectiveness of the US strategy.



“We just don’t know yet how effective it is. We are still in day two,” one analyst said.

The blockade, ordered by US President Donald Trump after failed peace talks, is aimed at stopping all maritime trade linked to Iran and forcing Tehran back to negotiations.

But it also risks escalating tensions in a region already on edge, with a fragile ceasefire due to expire within days.

Washington is targeting Iran’s oil lifeline – a sector that accounts for the vast majority of its economy – in what officials admit is a high-risk strategy.

Traffic through the strait has already collapsed from more than 130 ships a day to just a handful, with vessels halting, turning back or attempting to disguise their movements.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Iran has condemned the blockade as “piracy” and warned of retaliation, including targeting ports across the Gulf.

The move comes as Trump insists the war is “close to over” and a deal is still “very possible” – despite mounting military pressure and threats of further escalation if Iran refuses to abandon its nuclear ambitions.

News.title: Nanny who ‘killed’ baby after giving him medication to ‘sedate’ him is STILL working after ‘bungled cop probe’
News.content:
TOT TRAGEDY Nanny who ‘killed’ baby after giving him medication to ‘sedate’ him is STILL working after ‘bungled cop probe’

A BABY died after being given medication by a nanny who wanted to sedate him, an inquest has found.

The boy, who was just eight weeks old, was discovered unresponsive at his home by his night nanny – who is still working – on January 15.





An inquest into the tragic death also heard the coroner criticise the police and their handling of the case.

The hearing heard that emergency services were called at around 6.15am when the boy was in his bassinet.

The court was told upon their arrival that attempts were made to resuscitate him, but he was pronounced dead shortly after.

Toxicology tests later revealed the antihistamine chlorpheniramine was present in the baby’s blood.



Prof Fiona Wilcox, coroner for Inner West London, said: “This was probably administered to [the baby] by the night nanny”.

She added: “The baby had been described as unsettled and fussy and a baby who woke frequently in the night.

“The chlorpheniramine was probably administered to sedate the baby to sleep.

“Expert opinion accepted by the court was that this drug could possibly have caused or contributed to the baby’s death, but it could not be found that it probably did.”



The coroner recorded an open verdict.

The baby’s medical cause of death was listed as sudden unexpected death in infancy.

The inquest also heard concerns about how the police handled the case.

A report found officers “missed forensic opportunities,” including failing to seize feeding bottles or check bathroom cabinets for medication.

“The night nanny was not arrested and interviewed, nor was her property searched until October 2024.



“By then, of course, all forensic opportunities had been lost,” the coroner said.

“In this case it appears that they were reassured by the home environment and did not consider matters further.”

The toxicology findings only became clear after the post-mortem report was shared with the court, police and the family.

The nanny, who had been caring for the baby overnight on the second floor of the home, told the inquest she regularly attended training.

She also said she was still working as a nanny and registered with two agencies.



Prof Wilcox raised further concerns in a prevention of future deaths report.

She said there was “no national regulation system for nannies”.

She also suggested updating police training, along with guidance for nannies on administering medication such as antihistamines.

The coroner added that warning information on products containing chlorpheniramine may need to be reviewed.

A spokeswoman for the National Nanny Association said: “Parents are placing trust in individuals using professional titles, often assuming a level of training and oversight that simply isn’t required. That has to change.



“We have been calling for mandatory registration, clear standards and proper safeguarding checks for some time.

“This report reinforces just how urgent that need now is.”

A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said: “Our thoughts remain with the family of the baby following the conclusion of the inquest into their death.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We will consider the concerns raised by the coroner before providing a written response.”

News.title: Moment Starmer caught in Commons bust-up with Speaker as PM given dressing down over dodging Kemi’s questions
News.content:
THIS is the moment Sir Keir Starmer has a testy bust-up with the Commons Speaker after getting a dressing-down over dodging questions.

He is seen confronting Sir Lindsay Hoyle at the end of PMQs today, where he had been admonished for veering off topic.





At one point the Prime Minister can be seen hitting his fist against the side of the Speaker’s chair.

Tonight the Speaker confirmed that he has raised the problem repeatedly with No10 staff in private.

It comes amid Tory fury that the PM has been dodging Kemi Badenoch‘s questions in recent weeks.



Sir Lindsay Hoyle was forced to admonish the PM in the chamber today after repeatedly pivoting off points put to him by Kemi Badenoch.

He blasted: “Prime Minister, it is Prime Minister’s questions. We have got to concentrate.”

Tonight the Speaker’s office appeared to confirm their exchange at the end of the session surrounded the PM’s question-dodging.

A spokeswoman for the Speaker said that “answers should be confined to the points contained in the question.



“Every so often the Speaker has to remind Prime Ministers – and Ministers – of the rules of engagement in the Chamber.

“The Speaker has made this point to officials at No 10 on several occasions recently as well.”

In recent weeks Tory MPs have been furiously gesturing at the Speaker to insist he intervenes in Sir Keir’s potentially evasive answers.

The PM has repeatedly used questions on the Iran crisis to attack Ms Badenoch for initially wanting to support the American strikes.

Today he also accused her of the “mother of all u-turns” after being asked about when his Defence Investment Plan will be published.



Sir Lindsay’s spokeswoman said: “The Speaker is not responsible for the questions asked by Members or the answers given by Ministers.

“Questions to Ministers should relate to matters for which they are officially responsible.”

It is the third occasion that the Prime Minister has been reprimanded for not answering questions.



Last month, the Speaker said during PMQs: “I am sorry I am interrupting you, but unfortunately we have to stick to Prime Minister’s questions, not Leader of the Opposition’s questions.”

He picked Sir Keir up on the same point in January and said: “We do not ask the Opposition questions. These are questions for the Prime Minister, not the other way around.”

This comes as Sir Keir faces mounting pressure to reveal Labour’s defence investment plan for the next decade.

Today the PM avoided answering on when the vital plan might appear and ignored one question on a ship-upgrade plan.

Ms Badenoch used recent accusations from George Robertson as ammunition. The ex-Labour Defence Sec and former NATO chief slammed Sir Keir for delaying on defence funding and not providing key investment.



Lord Robertson said the government had left UK security in “peril” in a speech yesterday.

The PM disagreed with the claims and said the Labour party had committed to “the biggest boost to defence spending since the Cold War”.

Ms Badenoch retorted: “talking about an increase is not the same as giving an increase”.

She later referenced the Westminster summer of sex campaign in which Labour MP Samantha Niblett said she would bring sex toys into parliament in the hopes of improving education.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Tory leader told the Commons: “This is a moment of profound national seriousness. And what are they doing?



“They are promoting sex toys in parliament. That’s what they’re doing. It gives a while new meaning to fiddling while Rome burns.”

News.title: Families left vomiting over horrendous stench caused by 'sewage issue'
News.content:
Families left vomiting over horrendous stench caused by 'sewage issue'

People living in Chestfield, a small community outside Whitstable, Kent, claim they have been left unwell due to a stench emanating from an estate more than one kilometre away

View 4 Images Residents have spoken out about a pervasive smell that won't leave their community (Image: Facebook)

Residents of a small community in Kent say they have have been left vomiting, struggling to sleep and with watery eyes due to a "horrendous" sewage smell emanating from a nearby estate.

‌



Locals in Chestfield, just outside Whitstable, have claimed their lives are being made unbearable due to a smell they have said is being pumped out from the Oxenden Park development. Waste is being pumped through the estate, in Greenhill, near Herne Bay, and into the wider sewer network and Swalecliffe Wastewater Treatment Works.

‌



But the system isn't working as intended, reportedly due to low property occupancy rates, which have left wastewater sitting in local pipes.

‌



Serious disease found in waste water again this year, as experts issue warning READ MORE :

View 4 Images Oxenden Park is only around 41 percent occupied (Image: Bellway Homes)

Celena Campbell, 71, is among residents who have spoken up about the devastating impact the stench has had. She said that, although intermittent, the "absolutely horrendous" smell has started taking its toll on her mental health, and left another resident physically sick.

She said: “It makes your eyes water. It’s the worst possible smell you can imagine. One lady up the road was physically sick because of it."

‌



View 4 Images The smell from Oxenden Park left one resident 'physically sick' (Image: Bellway Homes)

“I don’t complain about my mental health lightly, but to be perfectly honest, I’m at my wits’ end because you never know when it’s going to be there. It’s really terrible.” While some attempts have been made to resolve the smell, including a temporary sewage disgestion fix, and the use of treatment chemicals carried out by developers Bellway, issues have seen it return.

The issue has become so pervasive that a group of residents staged a protest at the estate on April 12, among them Mandy Friend, who described the lengths she has to go through to disguise the smell.

‌



View 4 Images Chestfield is more than 1km away, but has been plagued by a smell from the estate (Image: Bellway Homes)

She told Kent Online: "It makes it really difficult to plan anything. You want to invite your friends over for a barbecue, but then you think, ‘They’re not going to want to come over if it absolutely stinks of sewage outside’. You end up going through bottles and bottles of bleach, and lighting scented candles, but you can’t even open a window because it comes in from the outside too.

"There are times that the smell is so nasty that it wakes you up at night." Bellway said in a statement to the outlet that it planned to have a temporary solution back up and running today so normal sewage flow may resume, with tankers having previously transported waste away from the estate.

Article continues below

A spokesperson said: "Bellway is aware of the issue raised and is working closely with our technical teams and contractors to resolve it. We are taking the matter seriously and steps are already underway to address the situation as quickly as possible."

News.title: British tourist swindled into paying £1,500 for kebab on popular beach
News.content:
British tourist swindled into paying £1,500 for kebab on popular beach

A brazen scammer allegedly charged a British tourist a staggering £1,500 for a kebab - and police near Copacabana beach, in Rio de Janeirom said the man was arrested

View 2 Images A British holidaymaker was charged £1,500 for a kebab (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

An unsuspecting tourist was hit with an eyewatering £1,500 charge for a kebab on a hugely popular tourist beach.

‌



A scammer was arrested on the world famous Copacabana beach, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, after he and another person allegedly changed the price on a payment terminal and overcharged the victim by a staggering amount. The Brit reportedly ended up paying £1,480 (10,000 reais) for the meaty treat that should have set her back just £15 (100 reais). Police said the machine was allegedly tampered with and ended up charging the victim a much higher price than what she was told.

‌



This comes as a wave of brazen conners have hit the popular Brazilian beaches in shallow attempts to swindle visitors. Brazilian police, in a statement, said: "We have arrested a criminal that carried out a card machine scam against a British female tourist in Copacabana."

‌



View 2 Images The woman was reportedly swindled on the world famous Copacabana beach (Image: Getty Images)

The detained man was reportedly part of an organised fraud scheme that targeted foreigners, mostly in Rio's famous Ipanema and Copacabana areas, according to O Globo.

The head of Rio's tourist police, Patricia Alemany, said her team (named DEAT) were working to find and detainee the people trying to con tourists out of their money, she told the Brazilian site.

‌



She said: "DEAT has been repeatedly arresting these criminals. However, there is no oversight of street vendors on the beach, which creates an environment of public disorder and greatly facilitates this type of crime."

Another woman was charged nearly £3,000 (20,000 reais) for corn on the cob which had been smothered in margarine. The woman, from Argentina, should have just paid £3 (20 reais) for the food. She said: "I don’t understand numbers in Portuguese. I don’t speak Portuguese."

Another tourist, from Colombia, was shockingly charged about £400 (2,500 reais) for a caipirinha - a Brazilian cocktail made with a spirit, sugar and lime.

‌



This comes after another shocking scam hit some tourists in Brazil. Last year, cases of "Goodnight Cinderella" spiking scams were reported, where holidaymakers fall for glamorous looking women, especially in Brazil, before they put powerful sedatives in victims' drinks and then rob them once they pass out.

The scams led to several Brits finding themselves with money, belongings and passports taken by the women who often work in gangs in popular tourist locations like Rio da Janeiro.

Police in Brazil said that British tourists are seen as "easy prey" as they could be unaware to the dangers, often have expensive items on them as well as cash, and do not know the local area well.

Article continues below

A 21-year-old Brit spoke out about how he passed out after taking just a few sips of a drink on his holiday. He was later recorded collapsing unconscious on a Brazilian beach but was rescued by a Good Samaritan. The student revealed he was offered a Capriahna cocktail by a trio women before the incident.

News.title: Airline files for bankruptcy as flights cancelled – but vital firm may be saved
News.content:
Airline files for bankruptcy as flights cancelled – but vital firm may be saved

Air Calédonie filed for bankruptcy while protestors blocked key airfields and caused flights to be cancelled, meaning the firm was losing an estimated £73,000 every day

View Image Air Calédonie filed for bankruptcy (stock) (Image: Getty)

A “vital” airline has filed for bankruptcy with flights grounded - but it could now be saved.

‌



Air Calédonie is the domestic airline for New Caledonia, a French territory in the South Pacific, and it filed for bankruptcy last month following a protest movement by customers in the territory's outer islands.

‌



The protestors blocked key airfields, angry at the company's decision to move Air Calédonie's operations from the Nouméa Magenta airport to New Caledonia's international La Tontouta base - more than 50km from Nouméa city.

‌



The blockade movement has aggravated Air Calédonie’s financial situation with an estimated loss of roughly £73,000 per day, making the company virtually unable to pay its staff in the short term.

Major UK car seller to shut down within days – more than 50 years in business READ MORE :

The crisis led to half its staff being placed on temporary employment and on part-time pay. New Caledonia President, Alcide Ponga, said of the action: "It looks as if someone wants the death of AirCal."

‌



Air Calédonie said it remained "mobilised to save a vital company for New Caledonia and design a viable recovery plan". The airline was founded back in 1954.

This week a Commerce Tribunal in New Caledonia started a judicially-supervised recovery process for the airline, according to RNZ.

This is despite the fact that talks held over the weekend with the leaders of the blockade collective and French State representatives failed to produce any progress.

Article continues below

Nouméa Commerce Tribunal, now effectively in charge of the airline’s affairs, said on Tuesday that the procedure could lead to a salvage plan for Air Calédonie.

Public Prosecutor Yves Dupas said this was probably the company's "last chance" to survive. The process could see Air Calédonie allowed to continue operations while debts from before April 14 would be “frozen”.

The aim is to "preserve" the company's cash flow as part of its "continuation of activity" for a six month period, which could then be renewed, hopefully meaning that eventually it will "have the means to recover to a sustainable activity level".

News.title: New fightback against 'scary' shoplifting gangs - from AI to citizens' arrests
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: New fightback against 'scary' shoplifting gangs - from AI to citizens' arrests

A report on ITV's Tonight reveals that shoplifting on an industrial scale is costing our retailers nearly half a billion pounds a year and forcing up prices for customers

View 6 Images An ITV Tonight programme reveals that the UK has a shoplifting problem - and it's costing shoppers millions of pounds (Image: Supplied)

Targeting high-value goods, thieves are clearing entire shelves, often stealing to order. Dr Emmeline Taylor, a broadcaster and professor of criminology, says: “It’s hugely impacting the retail sector, but also our communities.” Clapham in south-west London hit headlines this month, when scores of teenagers looted high street outlets. Now an investigation by the Tonight programme has examined the devastating effect of prolific shoplifting on small businesses and how they are fighting back.

‌



Sigga Redfern* launched a boutique in east London’s trendy Shoreditch eight years ago. Describing the shoplifting, she says: “It’s a massive problem. They just come, run in, grab everything they can and then run out again. They take the hangers, they take the alarms, they take all of it.”

‌



Theft costs Sigga, who cannot afford security guards, up to £1,000 a week. And she is forced to confront the shoplifters herself. Employee Ruth Evans*, 25, adds: “It’s quite scary, to be honest.” Ruth recalled a raid by four men in balaclavas, saying they took a whole shelf each. Sigga says some of her staff have been too scared to work there, adding: “They simply don’t feel safe.”

‌



View 6 Images Sigga's shop is raided by shoplifters (Image: Supplied)

She reports the raids, but says she is just given a crime number. The Metropolitan Police told Tonight shoplifting arrests increased by 50% last year and the number of cases they solved nearly doubled from 2024. A spokesman said: “Tackling retail crime remains a priority”

Dr Taylor, who is attached to City St George’s, University of London, says the reclassification in 2014 of stealing items worth less than £200 to “low-value shoplifting” by the Home Office attracted thieves to shoplifting. She adds: “Many offenders would say to me, ‘I’ve got a licence to steal, so long as I don’t surpass that £200’.”

‌



Cullan Mais from Cardiff was a prolific shoplifter for years, stealing vast amounts to fund his drug addiction. He says: “I was flat out shoplifting every single day. The only days I wasn’t shoplifting was if I was caught and was in prison. I’ve stolen in the millions. I used to think, ‘I’m just hitting the big corporate businesses and so be it’.”

View 6 Images Ruth, who describes the shoplifting at Sigga as "scary" (Image: Supplied)

Stealing to order, he would sell the items on. He has been arrested 30 times and handed 10 jail sentences. Cullan finally stopped five-and-a-half years ago, after quitting drugs, and now helps businesses to tackle shoplifting. He introduced Tonight reporter Paul Brand to a woman who began shoplifting at 12 and has served time for it.

‌



She steals items such as perfume, meat and alcohol to order, saying: “I’ll travel, so I don’t hit the same place all the time. I go from area to area, so as not to get noticed. I don’t steal from a corner shop. They’re family owned businesses. I do feel remorse, but at the end of the day, I’ve got to survive.”

A national police unit was launched two years ago to help coordinate investigations into organised shoplifting. But a survey by the British Retail Consortium suggests only 15% of retail crimes are currently reported. Jim Bligh, of the BRC, explains: “That number is so low because shopkeepers very often have low faith in the police.”

View 6 Images Dr Emmeline Taylor, a broadcaster and professor of criminology (Image: Supplied)

‌



In Truro, Cornwall, gift store owner Martin Ellis* invested in CCTV because of persistent thefts and dissatisfaction with the police response. He says he and the team started making “citizen’s arrests”, detaining shoplifters until police came. Martin says: “We’d explain to them that we had seen them taking something. If it came to it, we would hold on to them.”

The law around citizens’ arrests is detailed and complex. Detaining suspected thieves can be allowed, but it depends on the circumstances. But Martin says they have used them more than 50 times, making his business less of a target for shoplifters. He says: “We didn’t enjoy it. But we kept doing it and it worked.”

Devon and Cornwall police told Tonight it does not support retail staff carrying out citizens’ arrests, as it can be “dangerous for staff, customers and the wider public”. A spokesman said the force is now taking a more proactive approach to thefts. Martin said he is also supported now by a team of council and business-funded shop rangers, who patrol the city centre, gathering evidence to help tackle crime.

‌



View 6 Images Truro ranger Will Garside says: “We’ve got some pretty decent results – prison sentences, court orders.” (Image: Supplied)

Truro ranger Will Garside says: “We’ve got some pretty decent results – prison sentences, court orders.” Retailers are also using facial recognition in many stores, to log the identity of offenders, despite serious concerns from civil liberties groups. And many items – even chocolate – are now sold in security boxes, or on shelves protected by screens.

Dr Taylor says: “This basically makes it almost impossible to take the entire shelf.” At the Co-op, which has asked the government to tackle the issue of shoplifting and violence and abuse of its staff, the new security measures are having an impact.

‌



Campaigns director Paul Gerrard says: “We were seeing almost 1,000 incidents every single day. We’ve seen crime come down by 20% in total and we’ve seen violence and abuse go down by 35% in Co-op stores. The police have stepped up and we’re having an impact.”

View 6 Images James Roberts using the Armex Tech AI system (Image: Supplied)

David Brooks, the boss of a Leeds branch regularly targeted, adds: “We’re talking about groups of three or four coming in with massive bags and clearing the shelves.” Now, many of the most shoplifted items are in security containers. And staff in the kiosk work behind a secure screen.

‌



Minister for Crime and Policing, Sarah Jones, told Tonight shop theft is a “lawlessness that damages livelihoods”, claiming charges against offenders have risen by 21%. She said laws are being tightened and there were 3,000 more officers in neighbourhood roles. In Bridgend, South Wales, a convenience store plagued by shoplifters is trialling an AI system that flags potential shoplifting by analysing how customers are moving. James Roberts, from Armex Tech, says: “It detects suspicious gestures, i.e. hands going into pockets, or up jackets into bags.”

Cullan is advising the company on gestures to look out for. He says: “I’ve stolen in the thousands from this shop. With this system, you’re going to get caught.” Shopkeeper Simon Jehu adds: “It’s the instantaneous effect of it. The alert, it’s there. We’re aware of it in the moment, while the person is still in the shop, and we’re a much harder target because of that.”

*Shoplifting: Are We Paying The Price? is on ITV1 tomorrow night (Thursday) at 7.30pm.

Article continues below

*Surnames have been changed

News.title: Pablo Escobar's wild hippo herd to be hunted down and killed in Colombia
News.content:
Pablo Escobar's wild hippo herd to be hunted down and killed in Colombia

Pablo Escobar brought hippos into Colombia in the 1980s for his private zoo; the four of them mated, multiplied and then roamed freely around the South American country

View 4 Images Hippos are pictured at Hacienda Napoles Park, once the private estate of Pablo Escobar (Image: AP)

Colombian officials are set to cull 80 wild hippos from a colony originally started by Pablo Escobar. The notorious drug lord brought four of the animals into Colombia in the 1980s for his private zoo in the Magdalena River valley. They mated, multiplied and then roamed freely around the country. A study published by Colombia's National University estimated that there were around 170 hippos in the country in 2022. Environmental authorities say the mammals pose a threat to villagers who have encountered them in farms and rivers. Now the Government has said that around 80 of them will be culled in order to protect the environment and people who live locally.

‌



View 4 Images Hippos on the former Pablo Escobar estate (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Amanda Knox to travel to UK to promote film about Meredith Kercher's murder READ MORE :

England and Scotland among eight nations impacted by World Cup ban at host stadium READ MORE :

Environment Minister Irene Vélez said previous methods to control their population had not worked and proved expensive.

‌



They included neutering some of the animals or moving them to zoos. Announcing the cull, she said: "If we don't do this we will not be able to control the population. "We have to take this action to preserve our ecosystems." The animals are also competing for food and space against local species such as river manatees. But animal welfare activists have opposed the plan. Andrea Padilla, a senator who drafted a law against bullfights in Colombia, described he cull as "cruel".

View 4 Images The area has become a tourist attraction (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The hippos have made headlines over the years as officials think up different ways to deal with them. In 2022 they were officially declared an invasive species. The following year authorities began trying to neuter them.

‌



But the initiative had limited scope due to the high cost of capturing the dangerous animals and performing surgery on them. They have also become a tourist attraction with residents near the site of Escobar's former zoo offering hippo spotting tours and hippo-themed souvenirs. Colombia's hippos come from a limited gene pool and could carry diseases, so taking them back to their natural habitat in Africa has been considered unfeasible.

View 4 Images Pablo Escobar pictured in his heyday as a drugs lord (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Hacienda Nápolesm, Escobar's ranch which held the private zoo, was previously confiscated by Colombia's government and is now run as a theme park. Often called "The King of Cocaine," the drug lord was one of the wealthiest criminals in history. He was killed by police in 1993.

Article continues below

His cocaine empire made him one of the wealthiest people on earth. He was gunned down in his home city of Medellin by police on 2 December 1993, a day after his 44th birthday. Forbes listed him as the world's seventh richest man in 1989.

He had an estimated net worth of $9bn (£7bn).

His extraordinary story inspired a Netflix series.

News.title: Bristol 'murder' victim Jamie Collins, 21, described as 'gentle and kind' student
News.content:
Bristol 'murder' victim Jamie Collins, 21, described as 'gentle and kind' student

Jamie Collins, 21, was found dead in the garden of an address on Cleve Road, Filton, in Bristol, where he was "looking forward to finishing his university journey"

View 3 Images Jamie Collins is pictured (Image: FAMILY HANDOUT/UNPIXS)

The family of student who died from multiple stab wounds have described him as a "bright" and "unassuming young man" who had his "whole life ahead of him". Jamie Collins, 21, was found dead in the garden of an address on Cleve Road, Filton, in Bristol, in the early hours of Thursday. His family said the 'gentle and kind' student was "looking forward to finishing his journey" at at the University of the West of England (UWE).

He was due to return home to Swansea "in just a few weeks' time". On Sunday, police officers arrested fellow student Zack Coughlan, 23, a housemate of Collins.

He was later charged with murder and has appeared before Bristol Crown Court.

View 3 Images Forensic officers at the murder scene (Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach Plc)

"Words cannot describe how we are feeling as a family right now," Collins' family said. "We know he was heading for a hugely successful future following his engineering and robotics degree.

“We are continuing to work with and be supported by Avon and Somerset Police at this excruciating time.

“The outpouring of love and support from Jamie’s friends and ours has been completely overwhelming.

"We would like to thank everyone for their kind messages while we continue to grieve privately.”

View 3 Images The police at the murder scene (Image: PAUL GILLIS / Reach Plc)

UWE said Collins, a robotics student, was an "active member of student societies". "The university is deeply shocked by the news of our student Jamie's death in such distressing circumstances," it added.

Det Chief Insp Lucy Edgeworth, of the Major Crime Investigation Team at Avon and Somerset Police, said: “People who knew Jamie will be understandably shocked and hugely saddened to learn of what has happened.

“Neighbourhood officers have been carrying out high-visibility patrols in the area and are working closely with staff at the University of the West of England to ensure support is in place for those who need it.

Article continues below

“Further enquiries are planned in the area around Cleve Road over the coming days. We are grateful to people living in the area for their patience and understanding while we continue to carry out this investigative work.”

Coughlan will appear at Bristol Crown Court on June 19.

A provisional trial date has been set for October 12.

News.title: Russia issues 'sleep well' strike threat to three places in UK – see full list
News.content:
Russia issues 'sleep well' strike threat to three places in UK – see full list

Russia's defence ministry today issued locations of potential targets for strikes - including in London, Leicester and Suffolk - as Dmitry Medvedev joked 'sleep well'

View Image Vladimir Putin and Dmitry Medvedev (file) (Image: Getty Images)

Russia today made a direct threat to strike targets in the UK.

‌



Vladimir Putin’s defence ministry issued locations of what it alleges are production facilities supplying the Ukrainian armed forces with military equipment used to target Russian territory.

‌



Three of the addresses are in London, Leicester and Suffolk. Others are in multiple European countries. The move was “increasingly drawing these countries into war with Russia”, according to the ministry.

‌



Senior Kremlin official and former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev cautioned Western leaders that the threat should be “taken literally.” Medvedev is Putin's second-in-command on the Russian Security Council.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

“The list of European facilities which make drones [and] other equipment is a list of potential targets for the Russian armed forces,” he warned. “When strikes become a reality depends on what comes next... Sleep well, European partners!”

‌



The list specifies what appears to be Ukrainian missile maker Fire Point with an alleged address in Mildenhall, Suffolk, which is also the location of a RAF base. It operates as a key US air force hub. Alleged addresses in London and Leicester were also given.

“The leadership of several European countries, amid mounting losses and a worsening shortage of manpower in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, decided to increase the production and supply of UAVs to Ukraine for strikes on Russian territory,” said the Russian defence ministry.

“A significant increase in UAV production for the Kyiv regime is planned through increased funding for Ukrainian and joint enterprises located in European countries that produce attack drones and their components.”

Article continues below

The ministry said: “We regard this decision as a deliberate step leading to a sharp escalation of the military-political situation throughout Europe and the creeping transformation of these countries into Ukraine's strategic rear area.” It warned that “terrorist attacks against Russia” could lead to “unpredictable consequences”.

The Russian defence ministry also named alleged production facilities in Germany, Denmark, The Netherlands, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, the Czech Republic, Spain, Italy, Israel and Turkey.

Russian propagandist and British “expert” Vladimir Kornilov called it “an important and long-overdue warning from the Russian Ministry of Defence”.

News.title: Pet sitter and partner caught abusing two dogs while owners were on holiday
News.content:
Pet sitter and partner caught abusing two dogs while owners were on holiday

Pet sitter Paige Williams, 26, and her partner Bradley Regan Archer, 27, were caught on horrifying videos abusing two dogs when their owners returned from holiday

CCTV shows Solihull petsitter abusing dogs

A pet sitter and her partner were caught abusing dogs while their owners were on holiday.

‌



Pregnant Paige Williams, 26, of Kenilworth Road, Knowle, Solihull, and her 27-year-old partner Bradley Regan Archer have now been sentenced after shocking videos emerged of them dragging, kicking, hitting and screaming at dogs they were being paid to care for.

‌



Williams charged a family £1,400 to take care of their three dogs, two cats and two birds in July and August 2024. Archer joined Williams at the family’s Balsall Common home for what turned out to be weeks of animal abuse.

‌



When the family returned from holiday they watched horrifying footage captured on kitchen and garden cameras. They submitted 51 videos of evidence to the RSPCA which launched an investigation, BirminghamLive reports.

View 2 Images Commercial pet sitter Williams operated under the name Fur & Filly PetCare Services (Image: RSPCA)

All attacks involved their 13-month-old dog Ayrton and a three-year-old dog Frieda, both German Shorthaired Pointers. They did not relate to the third dog, the cats or the birds.

‌



Williams and Archer were caught on camera shouting and swearing at the dogs, dragging Ayrton and Freida by their collars, holding them off the ground, and pushing them through doorways and to the floor.

Commercial pet sitter Williams operated under the name Fur & Filly PetCare Services. The dog owners did not pay the invoice after uncovering the abuse.

In one clip, Williams appeared to address the owners directly. She said: "I will never look after your dogs again, my animals have suffered this month. My animals. I’ve had enough."

‌



The couple appeared at Coventry Magistrates’ Court on April 8 after Williams pleaded guilty to one offence of failing to meet the needs of two dogs under section nine of the Animal Welfare Act. Archer, previously of Balsall Street, Balsall Common, had pleaded not guilty and was due to stand trial but changed his plea on the day.

View 2 Images Williams and Archer were caught on camera dragging Ayrton and Freida by their collars (Image: RSPCA)

Magistrates sentenced Williams to a 12-month community order with 140 hours of unpaid work and ordered her to pay £350 costs and a £114 victim surcharge. Archer, who had stayed at the property throughout the four weeks, was sentenced to a 12-month community order with 40 hours of unpaid work. The court ordered him to pay £750 costs and a £114 victim surcharge.

‌



Both were banned from keeping all animals for seven years. RSPCA Inspector Ben Jones carried out the investigation on behalf of the animal welfare charity.

Speaking after the case, he said: "It’s a big decision to leave your pets in the care of someone else and, in this case, the family were leaving their pets with someone they felt they could trust.

"Sadly, Williams and Archer betrayed their trust with care that fell below the standards the law requires, with Ayrton and Feida subject to four weeks of abuse.

‌



"What made this case even more shocking is that they were clearly aware of the presence of the cameras and even appeared to speak directly to the dogs’ owners through the cameras amid such inappropriate animal care."

A vet, who watched the footage, said in a statement to the court that Ayrton and Frieda showed signs of anxiety and stress. She said: "Both dogs are handled in a way that would [have] negatively affected their mental welfare and their physical welfare."

In mitigation, the court heard Ayrton was a lively, young dog who could be challenging to deal with. Magistrates were told Williams was in the early stages of pregnancy at the time and was struggling to cope with hormonal changes.

Article continues below

The court heard the family had been introduced to Williams by a friend and had used her several times over the years, with no concerns, before asking her to have the animals. They left instructions to care for them as well as emergency numbers.

Mr Jones said: “They had no concerns about their pets until they returned home and found them to be quieter than normal, cowering if their son was too loud when playing. When they checked the cameras they were shocked by what they found.”

RSPCA said the dogs - who were ‘subdued, anxious and distressed’ when they were reunited with their family - were now doing well.

News.title: British doubles legend Jamie Murray retires from tennis
News.content:
Murray will be remembered for his razor-sharp volleying skills and the preposterous angles he conjured at the net. His returns were often unorthodox and he was fond of a lobbed service return to unsettle opponents.

Alongside his triumphs, Murray has been a staunch defender of doubles players and frequently demanded they be shown more respect.

"Doubles has its place in the game - it's not the golden ticket that singles is, but it's undervalued by the tour," Murray told BBC Sport.

"As these events go longer and longer they need content, and doubles supports that."

Murray said he was proud to have represented his hometown of Dunblane and the country of Scotland at the highest level.

"There is no history of tennis and no environment of tennis [in Scotland]," Murray told BBC Sport.

"I'd imagine the odds were against us from the start but we were able to make some good things happen."

His mother Judy thought Jamie had the better hand-eye co-ordination of her sons when young. Jamie and Andy briefly became rivals as tennis players - and also while wrestling.

Judy once recalled: "Andy's favourite [wrestler] was The Rock and Jamie's was Stone Cold Steve Austin, and they used to create these bouts that they saw on the television. They used to wrestle each other on the duvet and thump each other with pillows, and create these belts and make up their own rules and scoring systems."

Jamie is 15 months older than Andy, and as his early dominance on the tennis court started to fade Andy says he quite literally bore the brunt.

"We were coming back from Solihull in the minibus and I'd beaten Jamie in the final, I think, of the under-12s, so basically I was winding him up about that and my hand was on the hand rest," he said in 2015.

"We were sitting next to each other and he just basically punched me on the hand - I lost my fingernail and I've still got the scars to show for it."

He struggled with living away from home and the elite training environment, and even though he has never sought to blame the LTA, his forehand suffered and he has said he was never quite the same player again.

An 18-year-old college student was filming protests outside an immigration detention center in Los Angeles last month when an officer fired a projectile into his face, destroying his right eye and fracturing the bones in the socket.

Tucker Collins, whose damaged eye had to be surgically removed, has filed a federal civil rights complaint against Donald Trump’s administration, which faces an avalanche of lawsuits accusing federal agents of unconstitutional use of force after violent clashes with demonstrators across the country.

The complaint — which accuses federal agencies of assault, battery, intentional infliction of emotional distress and violations of California’s Bane Act, which protects protesters from threats of violence — demands $100 million in monetary damages.

“DHS has been turned into a weapon of terror, with no purpose other than to scare and brutalize,” Collins said during a press conference announcing the complaint on Wednesday

“I was recording when it happened. There was no warning,” he said. “One moment I was recording and the next thing I know, I can’t see. I’m on the floor, screaming in agony.”

open image in gallery Tucker Collins has filed a federal civil rights complaint after he was struck in the face by DHS agents’ less-lethal munitions during protests in Los Angeles ( Courtesy Tucker Collins/National Lawyers Guild )

Collins, a freshman studying astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California, was filming “No Kings” rallies on March 28 in downtown Los Angeles when he followed protests outside the city’s Metropolitan Detention Center.

Videos from the scene show Collins moving through the crowd with a camera before officers began firing crowd-control munitions into the crowd.

“I was blind for a couple moments,” Collins said. “I tried to swallow the pain as fast as I could, and be as clear and level headed as fast as I could. I remember feeling blood on my face.”

Other footage shows protesters wrapping Collins’s face in bandages while blood streamed from his face. Officers continued to fire tear gas in the crowd.

“It started to creep into my lungs,” Collins said. “I couldn’t see anything. I didn’t know what was going on.”

Images shared with The Independent show Collins in surgery as doctors removed parts of his eye and pieces of the object that struck his face.

A federal tort complaint, which precedes a lawsuit to be filed in the coming weeks, alleges officers began firing less-lethal munitions into the crowd — striking Collins from roughly 20 to 30 feet away — without any warning.

As a result, Collins has “suffered catastrophic and permanent personal injuries, including the surgical removal of his right eye, permanent vision loss, physical pain, psychological and emotional injuries, a traumatic brain injury, and significant economic losses,” according to the complaint.

Collins still faces multiple surgeries and will need to add another semester to his college education to complete his degree, according to his attorney.

open image in gallery Collins says he was merely filming demonstrations when DHS agents fired less-lethal munitions into the crowd, immediately striking his face. The injury required surgical removal of his right eye ( Courtesy Tucker Collins )

A spokesperson for Homeland Security did not respond to The Independent's request for comment about the complaint but stated that “the First Amendment protects speech and peaceful assembly — not rioting.”

“DHS is taking appropriate and constitutional measures to uphold the rule of law and protect our officers and the public from dangerous rioters,” a spokesperson said. “Our law enforcement has followed their training and used the minimum amount of force necessary to protect themselves, the public, and federal property.

A group of “1,000 rioters” surrounded the area and “threw rocks, bottles and cement blocks at officers,” who issued seven warnings to the crowd before deploying “crowd control measures,” according to DHS.

“I’m in no way an agitator. I just had my camera,” Collins said Wednesday. “There’s no way I was a danger to anyone.”

After Trump surged officers into cities to support his efforts to arrest and deport thousands of people from the country, protesters have reported devastating injuries including permanent vision loss, fractured skulls and broken ribs after they were hit with projectiles like pepper balls or tackled and beaten in the street.

Lawsuits against DHS in the wake of protests and dragnet-like arrests have prompted federal courts to intervene and block officers from indiscriminately firing into crowds with tear gas, pepper balls, rubber bullets and other weapons.

Protesters have accused officers of deliberately provoking crowds before firing into them and deploying excessive force at close range — actions that a judge in Chicago said “shock the conscience.”

Another recent blistering order from a judge in Oregon who blocked agents from shooting into crowds after children inhaled tear gas said “our nation is now at a crossroads.”

“When something like this happens, it really affects the whole family,” Collins’s mother Joann Collins said. “He was just there to document history … and they took his eye for it.”

Collins’s attorney V. James DeSimone has also urged state and local law enforcement to open a criminal investigation.

“Stop shooting at people’s heads,” DeSimone said. “How many eyes have to be lost? How many concussions do we need to have? How many injuries? … It is time to stop.”

Emma Grede has declared that women are held to “an impossible standard” while responding to backlash she faced for calling herself a “three-hour mum” on the weekends.

During an interview with The Wall Street Journal published earlier this month, the 43-year-old businesswoman said she’s a “max three-hour mum,” meaning she’s only with her four kids from 9 a.m. to 12 p.m. on each day of the weekend. She spends the rest of those two days focusing on activities for herself.

The remarks about her parenting choices were met with immense backlash online, which Grede addressed during a Tuesday appearance on Today. When the show’s co-host Sheinelle Jones asked if she was “caught off guard” by the criticism, Grede said she wasn’t.

“I just think that headline would never be written about a man,” the Skims founding partner explained, referring to the title of the WSJ piece, “The Kardashian Whisperer Who Says Three Hours With Her Kids Is Enough.”

“I think that's what happens to women is that we're held to such an impossible standard both as parents but also as businesswomen,” she continued. “What I'm trying to do is be really honest about what it takes and be really honest about the things I don't do. Because everybody says, ‘How do you do it all, ‘Emma? How do you wake up at five and run the companies?’

open image in gallery Emma Grede said she was not caught off guard by the criticism about her parenting approach ( Today )

“I'm like, let's give a list of all the things I don't do. Because you know what's helpful? That's what's helpful to women.”

Grede clarified what she meant by her “max three-hour mum” comment, noting that after going to work Monday through Friday each week, she’s exhausted by the weekend.

“Anyone who has children, you know that you don't spend eight hours on a Saturday and Sunday [with them]. You have errands to run, you have things to do,” she added.

She said that part of “being a parent” is giving her kids some freedom to do things on their own. “We're teaching our kids to be independent and, god forbid, how to actually entertain themselves,” Grede concluded.

Grede and her husband, Jens Grede, who got married in 2012, have an 11-year-old son, Grey, a nine-year-old daughter, Lola, and four-year-old twins, Lake and Rafferty.

The entrepreneur is raising her kids while juggling a busy career. She’s involved in multiple business ventures with the Kardashian family, including being the co-founder of Khloe Kardashian’s denim brand, Good American, and founding partner of Kim Kardashian’s shapewear brand, Skims.

open image in gallery Emma Grede works closely with the Kardashian family as the co-founder of Khloe Kardashian’s Good American denim company ( Getty Images for Emma Grede )

In her interview with WSJ, she said that on the weekends, she’s busy doing activities that “fill my cup.” With that in mind, she avoids reading school emails or engaging in activities that she believes are “overparenting.”

“Cutting sandwiches into star shapes? That was never it for me,” Grede said, explaining that her family’s team of nannies, cleaners, chef and chief of staff keep things running smoothly at home.

Instead, she wants to use her time with her children to create “high-impact, core memories,” such as fishing trips and vacations to New York.

She said that by establishing these parenting rules, she’s been able to manage a big family and successful career, like she’s always wanted. She’s also encouraged other women to write down their dreams and financial goals, while identifying things they wouldn’t ever sacrifice.

“I hold a vision for myself,” she added. “And I’m uncompromising.”
